# Z vs. t distributions

## Recall: z distribution assumptions

- z is just a normal distribution with mean = 0 and sd = 1.
- To convert a sampling distribution to a z-distribution, we need to know:
    - The true mean ($\mu$)
    - The true sd ($\sigma$)
- Problem: we don't know any of these!

## Solutions for unknown $\mu$ (from previous weeks)
1. Don't assume $\mu \rightarrow$ confidence intervals (can't say anything about probability)
2. Assume a fake $\mu$ (null hypothesis) $\rightarrow$ p-value (with probability)

- But what about unknown population sd, $\sigma$?

## Confession...
- We have pretended that only unknown $\mu$ matters
- But unknown $\sigma$ also matters!

## Solution for unknown $\sigma$ = t distribution
- The t distribution: a version of the z distribution that uses sample sd ($s$) instead of population sd ($\sigma$)

$$
Z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}
$$

$$
t = \frac{x-\mu}{s}
$$

- How? Use "degrees of fredom" ($df$) to make the t distribution wider $\rightarrow$ account for uncertainty in $\sigma$

-->

## Compare these plots

```{r}

library(patchwork)

a <- ggplot(data, aes(x=fear, color=mode)) + geom_freqpoly(binwidth=1)
fear_sd <- sd(data$fear)

b <- ggplot(data, aes(x=fear)) + geom_freqpoly(binwidth=1)
fear_sd <- sd(data$fear)

wider_data <- data %>% pivot_wider(names_from = mode, values_from = fear) %>% mutate(diff=flying-driving)

c <- ggplot(wider_data, aes(x=diff)) + geom_freqpoly(binwidth=1) +scale_x_continuous()
diff_sd <- sd(wider_data$diff)

a+b+c

```

- Hints: Look at x-axis. What are the main things to look for in descriptive statistics?
    - The spread of the differences plot is smaller than the spread of the fear plots.

# Paired t-test

## Difference between t-tests

- Normal t-test assumes that groups are independent $\rightarrow$ assumes the data has higher variance.
- Paired t-test assumes that there are pairings between groups $\rightarrow$ assumes the data has lower variance.
- Note: Paired data $\neq$ paired t-test! 
    - If you conduct a paired t-test on a dataset that is *not* paired, then the lower variance you get is misleading! You might be tricked into thinking you have stronger evidence than you actually do.

##

## `pivot_wider()`

```r
wider_data <- data %>% pivot_wider(names_from=mode, values_from=fear)

head(wider_data)

```

```{r}

wider_data <- data %>% pivot_wider(names_from=mode, values_from=fear)

head(wider_data)

```


## Code for paired t-test

- To do a paired t-test in R, use the following code:

    ```r
    t.test(data$A, data$B, paired = TRUE)
    ```

- This computes `t`, `p`, and `CIs` for paired data


## Key points
- Paird data: when groups are dependent on each other (e.g., correlation between individuals), they tend have lower variance.
- A paired t-test assumes lower variance in the data.
- Use paired t-tests for paired data.

    ```r
    CIs_paired = t.test(wider_data$flying, wider_data$driving, paired=TRUE)$conf.int
    CIs_unpaired = t.test(wider_data$flying, wider_data$driving, paired=FALSE)$conf.int

    compare_paired <- tibble(Paired=c("yes","no"), Mean=rep(mean(wider_data$diff),2), LowerCI=c(CIs_paired[1],CIs_unpaired[1]), UpperCI = c(CIs_paired[2],CIs_unpaired[2]))

    ggplot(compare_paired, aes(y=Mean, x=Paired)) + geom_point() + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=LowerCI, ymax=UpperCI))
    ```
- [ ] How are the CIs different, and why?
    - [ ] Think about the $SD \rightarrow SE \rightarrow CI$ pathway.

# What your results should look like

## t.tests
```{r}
t.test(wider_data$flying, wider_data$driving, paired=TRUE)
t.test(wider_data$flying, wider_data$driving, paired=FALSE)

```



## Paired/unpaired CI comparison
```{r}

CIs_paired = t.test(wider_data$flying, wider_data$driving, paired=TRUE)$conf.int
CIs_unpaired = t.test(wider_data$flying, wider_data$driving, paired=FALSE)$conf.int

compare_paired <- tibble(Paired=c("yes","no"), Mean=rep(mean(wider_data$diff),2), LowerCI=c(CIs_paired[1],CIs_unpaired[1]), UpperCI = c(CIs_paired[2],CIs_unpaired[2]))

ggplot(compare_paired, aes(y=Mean, x=Paired)) + geom_point() + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=LowerCI, ymax=UpperCI))

```

```{r}
sampling_dist <- c()

for (experiment in 1:1000){
    SampleSize=25
    driving <- rnorm(n=SampleSize, mean=0, sd=1)
    flying <- rnorm(n=SampleSize, mean=0, sd=1)
    sampling_dist[experiment] <- mean(driving) - mean(flying)

}

sim_df <- tibble(diffs=sampling_dist)

hist <- ggplot(sim_df, aes(x=diffs)) + geom_histogram()
```

```{r}

sim_dist <- c()

for (experiment in 1:1000){
    SampleSize=25
    person_effect <- rnorm(SampleSize, mean = 50, sd = 20)
    driving <- rnorm(n=SampleSize, mean=0, sd=1) + person_effect
    flying <- rnorm(n=SampleSize, mean=0, sd=1) + person_effect
    sim_dist[experiment] <- sd(driving-flying)
    sim_dist[experiment] <- mean(sd(driving),sd(flying))

}

sim_df <- tibble(diffs=sim_dist)

hist <- ggplot(sim_df, aes(x=diffs)) + geom_histogram()
hist

```


<!--

    - How would you modify to code to plot so that instead of a sampling distribution of the means, you get a sampling distribution of the t's?
    - How was x_obs calculated last week? How would you modify the calculation for x_obs to make it t_obs?
```{r}

x_dist <- c()
z_dist <- c()
t_dist <- c()

for (experiment in 1:1000){
    SampleSize=25
    driving <- rnorm(n=SampleSize, mean=0, sd=sum_table$SD[1])
    flying <- rnorm(n=SampleSize, mean=0, sd=sum_table$SD[2])
    mean_diff <- mean(driving) - mean(flying)
    pooled_sd <- (sum_table$SD[1]+sum_table$SD[2])/2
    experiment_sd <- (sd(driving)+sd(flying))/2
    x_dist[experiment] <- mean_diff
    z_dist[experiment] <- (mean_diff-0)/(pooled_sd/sqrt(25))
    t_dist[experiment] <- (mean_diff-0)/(experiment_sd/sqrt(25))

}

x_df <- tibble(diffs=x_dist, dist=rep("x", size=1000))
z_df <- tibble(diffs=z_dist, dist=rep("z", size=1000))
t_df <- tibble(diffs=t_dist, dist=rep("t", size=1000))


df <- bind_rows(x_df, z_df, t_df)

hist <- ggplot(df, aes(x=diffs)) + geom_histogram() + facet_wrap(~dist)
hist

```
